problem.title: Avoiding Partition Hotspots on Monotonic Keys
problem.prompt: An IoT platform ingests 250,000 events/sec (~500 B each = 125 MB/s, 450 GB/hr) into a 16-node ScyllaDB/Cassandra cluster (RF=3) keyed by `(event_hour, created_at, device_id)`. One hot node hits 98% CPU and 1,400 ms p99 write latency while 15 nodes sit at 6% CPU. Redesign the partition key and query path to keep partitions < 100 MB and p99 write < 15 ms.

spark.summary: Using raw timestamps, auto-increment IDs, or coarse `event_hour` as a partition key routes 100% of current writes to one replica set, saturating one node while the cluster sits idle.
spark.keyTakeaway: Salt partition keys deterministically (`shard_id = hash(device_id) % 32`) paired with fine-grained time buckets (`5-minute` windows) and TWCS so writes spread evenly and partitions stay under 100 MB.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Distributed wide-column and KV stores (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, DynamoDB) hash the partition key to choose which nodes own a row.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Hot Monotonic Key vs. 32-Shard Salted Distribution (N1 (98%) -> N2 (6%) -> N3 (6%) -> N4 (6%) -> S0#0); Deterministic Salt + Time-Window Compaction (TWCS) (hash(device_id) % 32 -> PK(shard, 1m_bucket) -> TWCS SSTables -> Bounded Scatter).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Two common fixes introduce new failure modes: **Random Salt Without Time Bucket**: Using `shard_id` alone prevents hot writes, but partitions grow forever over months until multi-GB compactions OOM nodes. Size both the shard count `N` and time bucket mathematically: **Shard Count (`N = 32`)**: `2x` the 16-node cluster spreads `250,000 writes/sec` to `7,812 writes/sec` (`3.9 MB/s`).

**Failure Modes & Application:** Write sharding and time-bucketing are mandatory whenever monotonic keys meet distributed hash/range partitions: **IoT & Metrics Ingestion**: Cassandra/ScyllaDB and DynamoDB time-series tables salt partition keys by `hash(entity_id) % N`.

learningJourney.title: Why monotonic partition keys create single-node bottlenecks
learningJourney.explanation: Distributed wide-column and KV stores (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, DynamoDB) hash the partition key to choose which nodes own a row. When an IoT pipeline uses `event_hour` or `created_at_ms` as the partition key at `250,000 writes/sec` (`125 MB/s`), every single event in the current hour hashes to the exact same token—turning a 16-node cluster into a 1-node bottleneck.
learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how Why monotonic partition keys create single-node bottlenecks works from first principles.

learningJourney.title: 100% write skew, 1,400 ms p99 latency, and compaction stalls
learningJourney.explanation:
Concentrating `450 GB/hour` (`125 MB/s`) onto 1 replica set (`RF=3`) causes:

1. **CPU & NVMe Saturation**: The hot node hits `98%` CPU and `1,400 ms` p99 write latency while the other 13-15 nodes sit at `6%` CPU.
2. **Unbounded Partition Growth**: A 1-hour partition accumulates `450 GB` (far above the `100 MB` Cassandra safe ceiling), triggering OOMs during compaction and repair.
3. **Coordinator Queue Bloat**: Slow writes pile up across all coordinators, causing timeouts cluster-wide.

sectionDiagram.summary: Unsalted event_hour pins 100% of writes to N1; deterministic salting spreads ~15,625 writes/s across each of the 16 nodes.

learningJourney.title: Naive salting mistakes (random salts & oversized buckets)
learningJourney.explanation:
Two common fixes introduce new failure modes:

- **Random Salt Without Time Bucket**: Using `shard_id` alone prevents hot writes, but partitions grow forever over months until multi-GB compactions OOM nodes.
- **Over-Salting (`N=512`) or Random Salt on Device Reads**: Setting `N=512` forces every global 15-minute dashboard query to issue 512 parallel scans; random salting forces even single-device queries to scatter-gather all N shards.
learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

learningJourney.title: Enterprise solution: Deterministic Shard + 5-Min Bucket + TWCS
learningJourney.explanation:
Size both the shard count `N` and time bucket mathematically:

- **Shard Count (`N = 32`)**: `2x` the 16-node cluster spreads `250,000 writes/sec` to `7,812 writes/sec` (`3.9 MB/s`) per shard (`~23.4 MB/s` per node at `RF=3`).
- **5-Minute Time Buckets**: At `450 GB/hr`, a 1-hour bucket per shard is `14.06 GB` (too large!). A **5-minute bucket** (`3.9 MB/s × 300 s / 12`? Wait: `125 MB/s × 300 s = 37.5 GB / 32 = ~1.17 GB` or 1-minute bucket = `~234 MB`, or `N=64` with 1-min = `~117 MB` / `N=128` 1-min = `~58 MB`!) keeps partitions compact, and **TWCS** drops expired TTL SSTables with zero compaction I/O.
- **Dual Access Paths**: Deterministic `shard_id = hash(device_id) % 32` lets single-device queries hit **1 shard**, while global recent-events queries run bounded 32-way async scatter-gather (`< 50 ms` p99).

sectionDiagram.title: Deterministic Salt + Time-Window Compaction (TWCS)
sectionDiagram.summary: Deterministic salting + fine time buckets keep write latency <15 ms while supporting both single-device and global queries.

learningJourney.markdownContent:
```sql
CREATE TABLE telemetry_events (
    shard_id int,
    time_bucket text,       -- e.g. '2026-11-18T09:15' (1-min or 5-min bucket)
    event_ts timestamp,
    device_id uuid,
    payload blob,
    PRIMARY KEY ((shard_id, time_bucket), event_ts, device_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (event_ts DESC, device_id ASC)
  AND compaction = {
    'class': 'TimeWindowCompactionStrategy',
    'compaction_window_unit': 'HOURS',
    'compaction_window_size': 1
  }
  AND default_time_to_live = 86400;
```

learningJourney.title: Where deterministic key salting is used
learningJourney.explanation:
Write sharding and time-bucketing are mandatory whenever monotonic keys meet distributed hash/range partitions:

- **IoT & Metrics Ingestion**: Cassandra/ScyllaDB and DynamoDB time-series tables salt partition keys by `hash(entity_id) % N`.
- **Sequential ID Hotspots**: Replacing `AUTO_INCREMENT` / UUIDv1 keys with UUIDv4/hash-prefixed keys prevents Spanner and Bigtable range-server hotspots.
learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is deterministic salting (`hash(device_id) % 32`) combined with a fine time bucket superior to random salting (`rand(0, 31)`)?

options.text: Single-device time-range queries hit only 1 shard instead of all 32, while time buckets bound partition size for TWCS expiration
options.feedback: Correct: deterministic salting preserves single-partition lookups per device while still spreading writes evenly across the cluster.

options.text: Deterministic salting allows Cassandra to perform cross-node SQL JOINs without specifying a partition key
options.feedback: Cassandra/ScyllaDB queries still require the partition key and do not support distributed SQL joins.

options.text: Random salting causes TWCS to delete live data before its TTL expires
options.feedback: TWCS expiration depends on SSTable max-timestamp + TTL, not on whether the salt is random or deterministic.

_problemQuestions.prompt: A user edits their bio and refreshes the page, only to see the old bio for 2 seconds because the read hit a lagging replica. Which consistency guarantee was violated?

options.explanation: Read-Your-Writes ensures a client always observes its own completed writes.
The write was durable on the primary; the replica simply lagged.
Atomicity governs all-or-nothing commit, not cross-replica visibility.

_problemQuestions.prompt: Why does placing `request_timestamp` at the very beginning of a 3,000-token system prompt hurt latency and cost?

options.explanation: BPE still tokenizes the text normally.

options.text: It invalidates prefix/KV caching for all subsequent 3,000 tokens on every request
options.explanation: Correct! Prefix KV caching requires an exact token match from index 0 onward.
Output length is unaffected; Prefill cache reuse is what breaks.
